d1_1a: This is the page you open every morning, and the only one you need to open. The greeting counts what's waiting.
d1_1b: Below it, the page is built in a fixed order, most urgent first: alerts that can't wait, your own reminders, today's calls, pop-bys, the monthly money check, your general tasks, and then every deal that needs something today. Work it top to bottom. When you reach the end, the day is won.
d1_2a: Alerts are the things that hurt if they wait a day: a deadline tomorrow, a signature request that's been sitting unsigned, an email the app couldn't match to a deal.
d1_2b: That last one is Mail to file — every reply to a deal email files itself, but when something arrives that the app can't place, it waits here. Pick the deal, and the email and its attachments move to it. An alert is only shown until you've seen it; the work itself lives further down, in the deal's card.
d1_3a: These are reminders you set yourself — from a deal's More menu, or by telling the assistant "remind me Thursday to call the HOA". They're yours, so they get their own loud section.
d1_3b: Done? Tap it. Can't today? Not Today pushes it to tomorrow, where it comes back on its own. Nothing you set is ever quietly dropped.
d1_4a: Your call list is really two lists. First, the promises: every time you log a call and pick a follow-up date, that person comes back on this exact day with the reason you wrote.
d1_4b: Promises always go first, oldest promise first — never sorted by how important the contact is, because a small lead that's about to buy is exactly the one that must not get buried. Below the promises is the rhythm list: people you haven't touched within their tier's rhythm. That's the system that keeps your whole sphere warm without you remembering anyone.
d1_5a: Here's the rhythm. In Contacts, you give each person a tier. A-plus and A are your best people — past clients, referral sources — and the app wants you talking to them every thirty days. B, every ninety. C, twice a year. D, once a year.
d1_5b: The app counts the days since you last logged a contact with them. The day the count passes their rhythm, they're due — and the next morning they're on your list, A-plus first. You never build a call list again. You just tier people once and keep logging.
d1_6a: The list is capped at fifteen promises and fifteen rhythm calls, and it's locked for the day the first time it's built — usually by your morning email.
d1_6b: A finished call stays on the list with a check and sinks to the bottom; a new name is never pulled in to replace it. Fifteen means fifteen, so the day can actually be won. Want more? Show ten more pulls in the next people due. Tomorrow you get a fresh batch.
d1_7a: After every call, tap Log and pick what happened. That one tap does three things. It records the outcome in the contact's history. It sets the next call date from the outcome and how hot the contact is — a hot lead you spoke to comes back in two days, a voicemail tomorrow, a sphere contact who said "not now" in ninety.
d1_7b: And whatever you type as the reason is what you'll read on this list when they come back. Change the date if they told you something specific — "call me after the fifteenth" — and that becomes a promise.
d1_8a: Promises pile up — you said you'd call back, life happened. The Follow-Up Review walks you through every overdue promise, one card at a time.
d1_8b: Call them now, keep it with a new date, or stop — some people are done, and that's fine. It remembers where you left off, so five minutes a day clears the backlog without it ever haunting your list again.
d1_9a: Two once-in-a-while items live here so you don't need a calendar for them. Pop-bys: your A-plus people are due a doorstep visit every ninety days, A every hundred and twenty, B every six months.
d1_9b: When someone's due, the tile appears and takes you to the Pop-Bys page to plan the run. And once a month, the money check asks you to upload last month's bank statement and confirm the numbers — five minutes, and your books are current all year.
d1_10a: General tasks are things that aren't tied to a deal — dues, signs, a class to register for. Add one from Tools, give it a date or not.
d1_10b: Dated ones show up on their day; undated ones sit under Next two days and undated so they're never out of sight. Done and overdue behave like everything else on this page.
d1_11a: Every deal that needs something today gets one card, with all of its items together, most urgent deal first. NOW is due or overdue. TODAY is due today. SOON is within the next two days.
d1_11b: Everything on these cards comes from the deal's timeline — the app reads every deal every hour and rebuilds this list — so you never have to open a deal to know what's due on it.
d1_12a: Cards aren't only timeline steps. A document that's required for this deal type and still missing shows with a Request-it button that emails the right person. Every week, the app prompts you to send your client an update — it drafts it, you approve. A listing sitting with no offers gets a price-reduction script.
d1_12b: A deal that started from your lead asks you to confirm it, so your numbers stay honest. A listing agreement about to expire warns you two weeks out. A past client's move anniversary comes up for a call. And when someone replies to a deal email, the app reads it and suggests the timeline update — you tap approve. Every one of these was found for you. Your job is the tap.
d1_13a: When you tick a step done here, it's done on the deal's timeline too — and the people who were waiting on it get told, in your name, without you writing anything.
d1_13b: Not Today snoozes a card until tomorrow morning; it never disappears. And if you finish everything, the page tells you so. That's the whole morning routine: alerts, reminders, calls, deals. Top to bottom.
d2_1a: Every deal is a card. The pill is its status — Active, Under Contract, Closed, On Hold, Cancelled. The bar is how many timeline steps are done for the phase it's in. A yellow badge means a required document is still missing.
d2_1b: A seedling means it came from one of your leads. And the sample deal — the one marked Sample — is a finished demo you can poke at; nobody on it has a real email, so it can't send anything, and it deletes itself when you have a real deal.
d2_2a: Read All shows only what's live — active and under contract. On Hold, Closed and Cancelled deals live in the dropdown so your list stays short. Leads shows deals that still need a first contact.
d2_2b: Flip to list when you have a lot. And on an active listing, Receive Offer is right on the card, because that's the moment you're usually on your phone in a parking lot.
d3_1a: If you have a signed contract, this is the fastest door. Upload it. The app reads the price, the effective date, the inspection and financing periods, the deposits, the closing date, and every person on it with their contact info.
d3_1b: You see everything it found before anything is saved — fix a date if it misread one, then approve. The timeline is built from those exact dates, and the reminders are scheduled. You can also send your client a link to upload it from their phone, no login.
d3_2a: No contract yet? New Deal asks three things: the address, who your client is and which side you're on — listing, buyer, or a lease — and the price with any dates you know. Save.
d3_2b: The right timeline builds itself for that type: a listing gets listing steps, a buyer gets financing and inspection steps, a rental gets its own. Rentals, new construction, commercial and land each have their own track.
d3_3a: Text a new buyer or seller your intake link. They fill it in on their phone — no login. Their answers become a lead on your deals list, flagged to call today, with everything they told you already on it.
d3_3b: A seller's answers even pre-fill the CMA subject, so you walk into the appointment with the pricing started.
d4_1a: The next step bar is the one line to read. It's the first timeline step that isn't done, with its date.
d4_1b: The status dropdown changes the deal's phase — and it's where Contract fell through lives, because that's a status change too, with a cleanup behind it.
d4_2a: Below it, the facts of the deal, and the Notes box — the one place for anything you'd write on a sticky note; the assistant writes here too when you tell it to. The Deal Doctor runs every night on every active deal: the risk level, what's stuck, and the one move to make, often with the email already drafted.
d4_2b: Run it again any time. At the bottom: cancel a deal and reminders stop, restore it, copy it to start a similar one, or preview exactly what your client sees in their portal.
d5_1a: The timeline is generated from the deal type and the contract's own day counts — the inspection period and financing days from the contract set the dates, not a generic template. Each step knows who it's for.
d5_1b: That's what drives the reminders: seven days out, three, one, the day of, and past due, to the lender, the other agent, or your client, in your name. Change a date here and the reminders move with it.
d5_2a: Tap the check when a step is done. Appointment steps — inspection, appraisal, walkthrough, closing — ask for a date and time first, then remind everyone who needs to be there, the day before.
d5_2b: Steps that match a document complete themselves when that document is uploaded. A missing document never blocks a step — you can always mark it done. And Reset and Rebuild regenerates the whole timeline if the deal changed shape.
d6_1a: The checklist at the top is your broker's required list for this deal type. Green is on file; amber is missing — a nudge, never a lock. Below it, everything is in folders. Upload a file and pick its type; it files itself and completes the matching checklist item and timeline step.
d6_1b: Drag files between folders, make your own, rename anything. Offers get their own folder, and a fallen-through contract's paperwork moves into a folder named after that buyer.
d6_2a: Share emails a document in your name and makes it visible in the client's portal. Get signature sends each signer a link with the sign-here stops already placed; you see who has signed; when the last one does, the stamped copy with its certificate files itself here — and if a request sits unsigned past the day it went out, you get a daily reminder and a card until it's done.
d6_2b: Read dates pulls the dates off any addendum and moves the timeline when you apply. And if your buyer waives the inspection, one button makes the release that records you recommended one, and sends it for signature.
d7_1a: Express asks four things: price, deposit, financing, closing. Full lets you set every term. Either way the app fills the official Florida AS-IS contract, adds the riders the deal needs — financing, HOA, lead paint on an older home — and builds one packet.
d7_1b: Save it and finish later, or send it for signature right here. Your buyers sign from a link; the signed packet lands in Documents. Regenerating a packet voids links already out, so send once.
d7_2a: When an offer arrives, upload it. The app reads the terms and parks it as pending — no emails go out. Each pending offer shows the seller's estimated net.
d7_2b: Share with sellers sends one link where they see every offer side by side and can accept or decline — you still make the final approve. Approve the winner: the deal goes under contract, the timeline rebuilds from that contract's dates, and the others are kept as backups.
d7_3a: Taking a listing? The Listing Package fills the official listing agreement and disclosures from the deal, bundles them for signature to your sellers and you, and the listing unlocks when the last signature lands. And if a contract dies: pick Contract fell through, choose why, confirm.
d7_3b: The whole contract record is archived for compliance, its documents go to a Fell-through folder, the other side's people come off, reminders and chases stop, and only the contract steps reset — the listing is back to Active. Backup offers resurface, and a reassurance email for your seller is drafted for your review.
d8_1a: Everyone on the deal goes here, once, with a role. The role is not decoration — it's what decides who gets which reminder. The lender gets the financing reminders. Title gets the closing ones.
d8_1b: Your own client gets the friendly version and the portal. Get the email right and the automation lands with the right people; that's the whole trick. Your client's row has their portal login link and a PIN reset for when they lose it.
d8_2a: Welcome emails introduce you and the deal to everyone — you read every one before it goes. Your client's welcome carries their portal link and, separately, a four-digit PIN; the link alone never signs anyone in, so a forwarded email can't leak the deal.
d8_2b: In the portal they see where the deal stands, what's needed from them, what happens next, the documents you've shared, and a way to message you. Sellers also see offers you've shared, with the net for each.
d9_1a: Direct is one person. Group is everyone you check, in one send — it goes out as email, as text from the team's number, and as a post in the deal chat.
d9_1b: Every email the app sends carries this deal's own address, so any reply files itself here. The deal also has its own inbox address — give it to the title company or the other agent, and anything they send lands on this deal.
d9_2a: When someone replies, the app reads it and, if it implies a timeline change — "inspection is Friday at ten" — it suggests the update; you approve or dismiss, nothing changes without you.
d9_2b: Texts come back to the person's most recent deal; if the app isn't sure, it flags it for you to place. And for emails people send straight to your own inbox, a one-time forwarding setup in your profile catches those too. Anything it can't place waits on Win The Day under Mail to file.
d10_1a: The seller's net sheet uses Florida's doc stamps and title costs and this deal's numbers to show what your seller walks away with — or, when the math goes the other way, what they need to bring to closing, worded honestly.
d10_1b: The buyer's version shows cash to close. Generate saves a PDF into Documents so you can share it.
d10_2a: Internal notes are yours alone — never in a portal. Reminders here are the ones that show under Your Reminders on Win The Day.
d10_2b: The activity log is the full trail of the deal: every email sent, every step changed, by whom and when — your record if anyone ever asks. And the CMA you ran for this property lives here too.
d11_1a: A contact needs a name and a phone. Two settings make the system work: temperature — hot, warm, cold, sphere, past client — which sets how fast the app calls them back after each outcome; and tier — A-plus to D — which sets the standing rhythm when nothing else is scheduled.
d11_1b: Import your spreadsheet from any CRM and map the columns once. The Tools menu holds the newsletter, your vendors, and the intake links.
d11_2a: Open anyone and you see everything: every call and what happened, every note, every email they opened.
d11_2b: From that history the app computes a Likely-to-Move score from zero to a hundred — how long they've owned, what they've opened, what they've asked, how your calls have gone. High scorers get the badge and a Win The Day nudge. Call them before they call someone else.
d12_1a: Pop-bys are small gifts on a past client's doorstep — the reason they call you, not the billboard, two years later.
d12_1b: The page lists who's due by tier, sets a budget per tier, suggests a gift, writes a note card for each, and maps the drive. Mark each one delivered, and it resets that person's clock.
d12_2a: Scripts give you the words, word for word, for the conversations agents avoid. Vendors is your trusted list — share a plumber with a client in one tap, by email, text, or both, and it posts into the deal chat too.
d12_2b: Calendar puts every closing, deadline and appointment from every deal on one month, click any one to jump in.
d13_1a: Money opens on the simple view: made, spent, kept. Commission from every closed deal posts itself.
d13_1b: Expenses come from your bank statement: upload it, the app sorts every line into a category, you glance and confirm. That's bookkeeping. Once a month, Win The Day asks you to do it.
d13_2a: Flip on Advanced when your tax preparer asks.
d13_2b: Expenses by category, income, a budget against actuals, a printable profit and loss for any date range, and the vendors you paid over six hundred dollars for 1099s. Same numbers, accountant's layout.
d14_1a: Type the income you want. The app divides by your average commission for closings, then works back through your own conversion rates — contracts per closing, appointments per contract, conversations per appointment — to a number of dials per day.
d14_1b: As your real numbers change, the plan updates. The five-year ladder shows where this year's habit takes you.
d14_2a: Reports come from what you actually did — the calls you logged, the deals you closed. The funnel shows where people drop off between "talked to" and "closed", so you know whether to fix the call, the appointment, or the follow-up.
d14_2b: Client feedback from the portals shows up here too, and so does your lead conversion — the seedlings you confirmed.
d15_1a: Run a CMA before there's a deal. Enter the subject and the comps; the tool does the adjustments and the pricing math and gives you a range.
d15_1b: The Seller Report is the two-page version for the appointment. Win the listing, tap Create Transaction, and the deal starts pre-filled from the CMA.
d15_2a: Every Florida form and rider, blank or already carrying your brokerage and license.
d15_2b: This is the same library the offer wizard and listing package pull from. Admins can add riders, and the app stamps and fills the supported ones.
d16_1a: Tap the question mark anywhere; type or talk. It can see what you can see — your deals, people, documents, messages, commission — and answer from them. It can also do things: add a note, complete or schedule a step, set a reminder, dial someone, draft an email — always showing you a confirm card first.
d16_1b: And it teaches: ask how to do anything and it walks you through the steps. One mic tap starts a hands-free conversation; say "no, that's all" to end it.
d16_2a: Help has the setup checklist, both tours, every step-by-step guide, and the FAQs. Feedback goes straight to us — use it for anything broken or confusing; we read every one.
d16_2b: And every page has its own one-minute clip of this tour in the bar at the top, whenever you need it.
d17_1a: Set your profile once — photo, signature, phone — and it's on every email, form and portal. Admins set the brokerage name, logo and colors, which brand everything clients see. Invite teammates by email and role.
d17_1b: Hand any deal to a transaction coordinator: they get their own portal for just that deal — full power to coordinate, never your commission numbers. And the Compliance Dashboard shows brokers every deal's required documents, with the required list and the checklist templates editable per deal type.
